_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 8 Mistakes Make Programs Better. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: the habit, more than one bug, mistakes become rules, a bug written down is an error, and a partner. The two-bug chapter is the lesson's own first round (shrink, jump, hide - programmed as grow, jump, spin) and its sprite sizes come from ART.run, the lesson's own arithmetic. Every mark in this film lands on a BLOCK, never on a person, and a fixed block fades into its own slot so nothing above it is disturbed.
title: Mistakes Make Programs Better
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Know how to test and debug programs so that they run and produce the desired output.
Understand that programmers use their mistakes to inform the programs that they create.
Outline the benefits of working with others when creating programs.

beats.say: You run your program, and the cat spins when it should have jumped.
That is a bug. Finding it and fixing it is called debugging.
Debugging is not luck. It is a habit with five steps, every time.
Run it first. You cannot fix what you have not seen.
Look: where did it go wrong? Think: which block did that?
Fix that one block, not the whole program. Then run again.
It is easy to skip look and change the first block you see.
Watch where it went wrong. The bug is there.
The cat should shrink, then jump, then hide. That is what you wanted.

at.goal: should shrink, then jump, then hide

beats.say: Run it. The cat grows, jumps, and then spins. Two blocks are wrong.
The first block grows. You wanted shrink, so that block is the bug.
Fix it to shrink and run again. The cat still spins at the end.
The second bug was hiding behind the first one all along.
Change spin to hide, run again, and the cat does what you wanted.
Every programmer makes mistakes. Good ones write them down as rules.
The cat began in the wrong place. The rule: reset first.
The repeat repeated the wrong block. Check the block after it.

at.repeat: The repeat repeated the wrong block

beats.say: You fixed a bug and never ran it. Run again after every fix.
Your next program is better because of the last one's mistakes.

scenes.heading: A bug written down is an error

beats.say: Programmers say bug when they are talking to each other.
Written down properly, a mistake in a program is called an error.
You report the error: what you expected, and what actually happened.
Then you debug it. The two words go together.
Every program ever written has had errors. Somebody kept looking.
Your partner did not write your program, so they read every block.
You skip the blocks you are sure about, and one of those is the bug.

at.bug: one of those is the bug

beats.say: Explain it to them out loud, block by block.

at.explain: Explain it to them out loud

beats.say: Halfway through you stop: it should not spin. You found it yourself.
One of you presses Run. The other watches, and sees it go wrong.
Debugging is a habit: run, look, think, fix, run again.
A bug is a mistake in a program. Written down, it is an error.
Every mistake gives you a rule for your next program.
And fresh eyes find the block you keep skipping. Ask a partner.
